title: Trajectory Statistics Govern Mechanical Power Transfer in Active Baths
authors: Chul-Ung Woo, Jiwon Choi, Heiko Rieger
abstract: The mechanical response of a moving probe in an active bath reflects both the dynamics of the bath and how the probe couples to it. For a probe moving at velocity $\mathbf V$ and interacting weakly with an ideal active bath, we show that the trajectory statistics of a free bath particle determine a density response from which the bath force on the probe follows. The probe-particle interaction determines how this response is weighted over wave vector $\mathbf q$, while the probe motion selects frequencies $ω_{\mathbf q}=\mathbf q\cdot \mathbf V$. This trajectory-response relation separates the bath dynamics from the wave-vector weighting, so neither the stationary state nor force correlations need to be recalculated for each probe interaction and velocity. Applying this relation to active-particle models, we prove that positive power transfer is excluded for active Ornstein--Uhlenbeck particles in all dimensions and for complete-reset run-and-tumble particles in $d\geq2$, while one-dimensional run-and-tumble particles and two-dimensional active Brownian particles possess modes that can transfer positive mechanical power. For a given probe, this response predicts drag reversal, spontaneous probe motion, and motion-induced density distortions, all in quantitative agreement with simulations. Varying the probe geometry changes how the same bath response is weighted, thereby selecting different moving states. Beyond the leading weak-probe, ideal-bath limit, higher orders in probe strength involve multi-interval trajectory statistics, while finite-density corrections involve interacting-particle dynamics. Our results connect the trajectory statistics of active bath particles to the mechanical response of a passive probe, providing a route to predict probe response from single-particle trajectory statistics measured in the absence of the probe.
summary: This paper develops a theoretical framework showing that the mechanical force and power transferred by an active bath to a probe are governed by the bath's single-particle trajectory statistics. By analyzing specific active models, the authors determine the conditions under which positive power transfer (energy injection) can occur, providing quantitative predictions for phenomena like drag reversal.
main_problem: The paper determines the mechanical force and power transfer exerted by an active bath on a moving probe, linking this response directly to the single-particle trajectory statistics of the bath particles.
main_result: The sign of the mechanical power transfer depends critically on the specific dynamics of the active bath; for instance, 1D run-and-tumble particles and 2D active Brownian particles can exhibit modes that transfer positive mechanical power, while AOUPs and 2D+ RTPs do not.
method: The authors derive a trajectory-response relation that separates the bath dynamics from the wave-vector weighting, allowing the calculation of the force and power using the free-particle self-intermediate scattering function (ISF).
model_or_system: The system consists of a passive probe moving at velocity V immersed in a dilute, ideal gas of noninteracting active particles, modeled using dynamics like Active Ornstein-Uhlenbeck processes, Run-and-Tumble Particles, and Active Brownian Particles.
key_observables: Mechanical force $F_{	ext{bath}}(V)$, mechanical power transfer $\dot{W}_{	ext{bath}}(V)$, density response $\deltaho(\mathbf{r}; V)$, and the self-intermediate scattering function $\Phi_0(q, t)$.
important_parameters: Probe velocity $V$, wave vector $q$, and the dimensionality $d$ of the system.
main_assumptions: The analysis is performed at the leading weak-probe, ideal-bath limit, linearizing the response in the probe potential, and assuming non-interacting bath particles.
figures_summary: The notes do not describe specific figures, but mention that the analysis predicts phenomena like drag reversal, spontaneous probe motion, and motion-induced density distortions.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the theoretical framework connecting force to trajectory statistics, derives the power transfer criterion, and then applies this framework to analyze specific active particle models (AOUPs, RTPs, ABPs) to determine the sign of energy transfer.
why_interesting: This work provides a powerful, general theoretical tool—the trajectory-response relation—to predict macroscopic mechanical forces and energy flow in complex active matter systems solely from single-particle statistical measurements.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. From free-particle motion to the mechanical response of a moving probe. The moving-probe problem separates into a bath response determined by the free-particle self-ISF, frequency sampling set by the probe velocity, and wave- vector weighting set by the probe-bath interaction. The right panels illustrate the sampled responses for two probe velocities together with the interaction weight. Combining them in the force integral gives the bath force and the mechanical power transferred from the bath to the probe.

FIG. 2. Dimension-dependent response of active Brownian particles. (a,b) Rescaled responses Hd(z, Ω) for (a) d = 2 and (b) d = 3, evaluated from converged trunca- tions of the angular hierarchy. The two-dimensional response contains a region with Hd < 0, corresponding to modes that can transfer positive mechanical power, whereas the three- dimensional response remains positive throughout the dis- played domain. (c) Numerical checks of the analytical asymp- totic limits of Hd(z, 0). (d) Deviation 1 −md of the minimum from unity. The numerically obtained minima approach the static large-d scaling 18/d2.

Figure 3 compares the finite-frequency responses of the three matched active-particle models in the common di- mensionless variables (z, Ω). The one-dimensional RTP and two-dimensional ABP contain regions with KX d < 0, whereas the AOUP response remains nonnegative. Linear friction depends only on KX d (z, 0). At nonzero imposed speed, a mode making an angle φ with the probe velocity samples the response at Ω= (V/v0)z cos φ. In one dimension, this sampling reduces to |Ω| = (|V |/v0)z. In dimensions d ≥2, the angular degree of freedom allows |Ω| ≤(V/v0)z at each z. Modes with sufficiently small | cos φ| can sample small frequencies even for V > v0.

FIG. 3. Finite-frequency response of standard ac- tive baths. Dimensionless responses KX d (z, Ω) for (a) a one- dimensional RTP, (b) a two-dimensional ABP, and (c) a two- dimensional AOUP. Here z = qv0τ and Ω= ωτ. Only Ω≥0 is shown because inversion symmetry makes KX d even in fre- quency. Color denotes the response on a symmetric logarith- mic scale, and solid black contours mark KX d = 0. The dashed line Ω= z corresponds to V = v0 with q ∥V .

FIG. 4. Linear friction for Gaussian probes in matched ideal active baths. Friction coefficient per bath density, γ/ρ0, as a function of Γ = v0τ/a for (a) a one-dimensional RTP, (b) a two-dimensional ABP, and (c) a two-dimensional AOUP. Solid curves are the V →0 weak-potential predictions obtained by integrating the corresponding responses at Ω= 0 over wave number with the Gaussian interaction weight. Open circles show direct fixed-velocity simulations at V/v0 = 0.01. Horizontal dashed lines indicate zero friction. The RTP and ABP friction coefficients change sign at ΓRTP c,1 and ΓABP c,2 , re- spectively, whereas the AOUP friction remains positive.
